data.title: The Nvidia Mess—and What It Means for the Stock
data.description:
The serious dustup over Nvidia chip exports to China exploded this week with a gripping story involving Nvidia’s founder and (now former) CEO Jensen Huang.

Specifically, a romantic relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), an alleged Chinese spy and CEO of a Singapore-domiciled company that is an Nvidia client. It seems that some advanced Nvidia chips eventually made their way from Singapore to China.

Importantly, the Wall Street Journal reported that as recently as the summer of last year, Singapore was one of Nvidia’s biggest markets, generating 22% of the chip maker’s revenue, up 81% from a year earlier. Then, it abruptly disappeared from the company’s financial disclosures.

This revelation ties together the current U.S. advanced chip export ban to China plus the possibility that classified intelligence regarding either the U.S. government or Nvidia was compromised.

The media is intensively following up on this, and other allegations are possible. Senators Warren and Coons are already in action regarding hearings.

The Nvidia mess could also negatively impact the forthcoming Anthropic (ANT) IPO.

[text_ad]

This story is evolving day by day as Nvidia (NVDA) stock is already down sharply over the last month. The downside risk is significant, and the blast radius in the AI world and Washington will widen considerably if it is confirmed that Jensen Huang shared sensitive or classified information.

Nvidia is at the center of AI – the linchpin of the AI story.

Due to the company’s dominant market position in advanced AI chips, a strong balance sheet, close ties to Washington power players, a high growth rate, and extensive circular vendor and shadow financing, it is also essentially the central bank of AI, something that Bloomberg explored in great detail last year.

It is fine to buy some Nvidia (NVDA) stock on current weakness, but I advise caution as events can take an uncertain turn and the Nvidia board has already taken the step of naming a replacement interim CEO, Colette Kress.

Regarding Alice Huang, more and more is coming out regarding her past operations and connections to a wide variety of Chinese businesses and organizations.

The infographic on this page from The Wire China connects the dots.

Chinese tech firms are now leapfrogging across industries and sectors, moving from smartphones to EVs to robotics. EVs, drones, and robotics share many of the same core components, like batteries, sensors, and electronic controllers. These days, nearly every major Chinese tech firm has its own AI models, custom chips, and robots. You might call them physical AI conglomerates. Xiaomi (XIACY) recently claimed to have its own humanoid robots doing autonomous 8-hour shifts on its EV production line.

The chief benefactor of the Nvidia mess is China, and particularly Huawei. In 1984, Shanghai Bell was the first China telecom equipment joint venture, and other joint telecom ventures with foreign companies soon followed, including Huawei. By the 1990s, China had successfully shifted from importing telecom equipment to producing most of it domestically through these joint ventures.

Huawei now stands at the heart of China’s advances and ambitions. Founded in 1987 as a small supplier of telephone switches, Huawei has transformed into a manufacturing and digital giant with over $100 billion a year in revenue. A partial subsidiary is currently providing undersea cables connecting three continents and semiconductor chips.

It is time for a new, permanent Nvidia CEO to bring in a new, tighter operating system. The stock may rise on such an announcement.

[author_ad]

data.title: Is the AI Trade Over? 1 Defensive Stock to Buy Instead
data.description:
Is the AI trade over?

No one knows for sure, but economist and market strategist Jim Paulsen thinks it could be.

He points out that the relative performance of AI stocks has been leading the increase in the ratio of New Era spending to real GDP since early 2023. It follows that the current underperformance of AI stocks could be warning of a significant decline in New Era spending compared to overall real GDP going forward. After all, stocks typically anticipate economic and sector trends – as was the case during the AI boom time of the past three years.

If he’s right, it makes sense to tilt your portfolio more towards “old era” non-AI stocks. They’ve been vastly outperforming AI stocks in the past month. During that time, his S&P 500 Old Era Stock Price Index (comprising a market cap weighting of the nine S&P 500 sectors excluding the New Era technology & communications sectors) has risen by 4.2%, compared to a 27% decline in the Bank of America AI Beneficiaries Index. This could be the start of a trend that has old-era stocks outperforming AI stocks going forward.

Old-era stocks have a lot of ground to make up. They made up 80% of the S&P 500 ten years ago, compared to just 50% in early October, Paulsen points out in his Paulsen Perspectives on Substack.

A Defensive Dividend Stock to Buy if AI Stocks Keep Falling

PepsiCo (PEP)

If you want to diversify away from AI stocks in favor of old-era and more defensive names, consider owning PepsiCo. Snack foods and fizzy drinks are about as far away from AI as an investor could get.

Shares of the brand powerhouse were recently down around 20% from their early February highs.

In the weakness, a director who knows the snack and soft drink space quite well because of a lifetime of experience in the business and at PepsiCo stepped up to buy $23.7 million worth of stock.

The purchase makes sense because there are good reasons to think that PepsiCo results may improve from here.

Investors doubt a mini turnaround in the works will pan out. Buying shares here is a bet they will be wrong. I think it is a good bet, given the director’s enthusiasm for the stock.

PepsiCo is doing some renovation work in its kitchens, and improvements to the business look like they will boost sales performance from here. That’s clearly what this director is counting on, with his huge purchase.

Third-quarter sales overall grew 5.6%, which doesn’t sound terrible. But organic growth was only 3.1%. The rest came from one-offs like acquisitions and divestitures and foreign exchange benefits.

Drilling down, international sales were up 8% and North American beverage and food sales were roughly flat. This tells you what you need to know about the growth opportunities from here. Expect further strength abroad as the company continues to invest in growth in Latin America, Asia, and Africa. The renovation work at home in North America should continue to boost results there.

North America

Let’s focus on what’s going on in North America, since this is where the biggest opportunity for improvement lies. Growth has slowed down over the past two years, mainly due to sluggish performance as the GLP-1 effect continues to hit sales, and consumers generally turn more health conscious and buy less due to rising costs overall.

The company is taking steps to stem the tide.

It is making products more affordable. In snacks, it is innovating by adding more natural ingredients to make products appear healthier. In beverages, the company is developing in-house brands and looking to brand licensing to expand its presences in non-sparkling categories. It is also investing more in digital marketing.

The tweaks seem to be working. Volumes improved in the third quarter. In food, volume was flat compared to down 2% in the second quarter. Drink sales volume contracted by 2% compared to 4%. Management guides for further improvement. Though like all turnarounds, this one will take time.

[text_ad]

Natural Strengths

PepsiCo has some natural strengths that support both the turnaround effort and the investment thesis.

* Besides the powerful brands, its sheer size ($94 billion in revenue) gives it huge distribution and procurement clout.

PepsiCo ranks number one in the $247 billion global savory snacks market, according to Euromonitor, thanks to well-known brands such as Lay’s, Cheetos, and Doritos. It controls 22% of this space. In drinks, PepsiCo is the world’s second-largest beverage provider behind Coca-Cola (KO), offering popular brands like Gatorade, Pepsi-Cola, and Mountain Dew.

Not surprisingly, the company has close relationships with retailers. Its brands drive foot traffic, making PepsiCo a must-have partner to most retailers. In return, it gets favorable shelf placement.

All of these advantages give PepsiCo a wide moat.

* PepsiCo has defensive characteristics which suggest the stock will hold up if the tech pullback continues, or if we do go into a phase of economic weakness.

* PepsiCo is in excellent financial health. It has a solid balance sheet and strong free cash flow backing a 4.2% dividend yield. It is a net debt/EBITDA ratio of 2.7, which is fairly conservative.

The bottom line: PepsiCo is undervalued, as investors doubt its ability to restore consistent profit growth. Its current price-to-sales ratio of 2 is 21% below the trailing five-year average. The forward price-to-earnings ratio of 16.9 is a 19% discount to the five-year average of 20.9. I suggest betting against the negative investor sentiment, alongside the director who just made a massive stock purchase.

Director Robert Pohlad, with his $23.7 million purchase, is betting these valuation gaps will close as international growth continues and the mini-turnaround continues to bear fruit. He’s worth listening to because he knows the space so well. Pohlad served as chairman and CEO of PepsiAmericas from 2002 until PepsiCo acquired it in 2010. He worked at various PepsiCo distributors for years before 2002. Pohlad, who, along with his family, owns the Minnesota Twins, has been a PepsiCo director since 2015.

For more “old era” names to consider owning for outperformance because insiders love them, subscribe to Cabot Insider Edge.

[author_ad]

data.title: 5 Tech Stocks Hitting 52-Week Highs in the AI Correction
data.description:
The artificial intelligence (AI) boom has hit a wall. After years of impressive gains, investors are starting to question whether the hundreds of billions of dollars being spent on AI infrastructure will generate enough profits to justify the investment.

Those concerns have triggered a sharp selloff in some of the market’s biggest technology stocks.

As of Friday’s close, AI chip giant Nvidia (NVDA) had plunged 24% in the last month, while semiconductor powerhouse Broadcom (AVGO) had fallen 22%. Other AI-related stocks have suffered similar losses over the last one-month period, including Palantir Technologies (PLTR), down 19%, and Meta Platforms (META), down 18%.

The Nasdaq recently entered correction territory, falling more than 10% below its October high while being dragged down by some of the biggest beneficiaries of the AI boom.

But not every technology stock is struggling.

Right now, a grand total of six technology stocks are hitting 52-week highs as the broader technology sector stumbles.

Of note, one of those six technology stocks is STRC, Strategy’s preferred C shares, the Bitcoin-linked preferred stock that appeals to investors for its yield and not its potential for upside momentum.

So, excluding STRC, that leaves us with just five technology stocks that are truly bucking the AI correction. Let’s take a closer look.

[text_ad]

5 Tech Stocks Bucking the AI Selloff

Consensus Cloud Solutions (CCSI)

Consensus Cloud Solutions (CCSI) is one of the most surprising technology winners of 2026. The stock has nearly doubled this year and is currently trading at a 52-week high.

Consensus provides secure digital communications services, including cloud faxing and document delivery. Its products are particularly valuable in healthcare, government and other industries where secure information exchange is essential.

The company’s third-quarter results demonstrated the appeal of predictable recurring revenue. Revenue increased 3.7% to $91 million, while its corporate business grew 9.1%. Adjusted EBITDA reached $47.6 million, representing an impressive 52.3% margin.

Consensus also continues to repurchase shares, buying back approximately 550,000 during the quarter.

The appeal here is straightforward. Investors get a profitable technology company with recurring revenue and strong margins without paying the premium valuations associated with many AI stocks.

Shares have risen 79.5% so far this year and 20.3% over the course of the one-month correction in the Nasdaq.

JFrog (FROG)

JFrog (FROG) is a much more direct beneficiary of the AI revolution.

The company provides software development tools that help businesses manage, secure and distribute their software applications. Its platform helps developers keep track of the software components used in applications and ensure they’re ready for deployment.

That business is becoming increasingly important as AI transforms software development.

AI-powered coding tools can generate enormous amounts of code in a fraction of the time typically demanded of human programmers. But someone still needs to organize, secure and manage all that software.

That’s where JFrog comes in.

The company’s third-quarter results highlight its relevance. Revenue jumped 31% from a year earlier to $179.2 million. Cloud revenue surged 60% to $101.5 million, accounting for 57% of total revenue.

Meanwhile, the number of customers spending more than $1 million annually increased 58% to 112.

Investors liked what they saw. JFrog shares soared more than 35% on November 6 following the earnings announcement, putting the stock back near its record high and pushing the one-year return to 63.2%.

JFrog offers an interesting alternative to the traditional AI trade. Rather than betting on which chipmaker or AI model will ultimately dominate, the company provides tools that businesses need as software development becomes faster and more complex.

But, as with many AI-related names, the biggest concern is valuation, as JFrog is not yet consistently profitable and is trading at an astronomical forward P/E of 90.6.

NIQ Global Intelligence (NIQ)

NIQ Global Intelligence (NIQ), better known as NielsenIQ, is another technology company benefiting from the growing demand for data and analytics.

The company helps retailers and consumer products businesses understand what people are buying, where they’re shopping and how their purchasing habits are changing.

Its enormous collection of consumer data is particularly valuable in the age of artificial intelligence.

AI systems become more useful when they’re trained on reliable, specialized information. NIQ possesses a wealth of proprietary consumer purchasing data that can help businesses make better decisions about pricing, marketing and inventory.

And unlike many emerging AI businesses, NIQ already generates billions of dollars in annual revenue.

Second-quarter revenue increased 8% to $1.12 billion, while adjusted EBITDA climbed nearly 22% to $261.9 million. The company also raised its full-year financial guidance.

Importantly, NIQ is improving profitability and cash generation while continuing to expand its subscription-based intelligence business.

The stock is up 60% in the last year (although it’s worth noting that those returns are on the heels of the company’s post-IPO droop, as it came public in July 2025; the stock is up only 4.1% since the IPO) and recently traded near its highest levels since going public in July 2025.

Block (XYZ)

Block (XYZ), formerly known as Square, is best known for its Cash App digital payments platform and Square payment-processing systems.

But the financial technology company is also becoming increasingly focused on artificial intelligence.

Block is incorporating AI into its products to help merchants manage their operations and consumers make better financial decisions. It also sees opportunities to improve internal efficiency through automation.

More importantly, its underlying businesses are performing well.

Third-quarter gross profit grew 22% to $3.24 billion. Adjusted operating income soared 92% to $923 million, while adjusted earnings per share more than doubled to $1.13.

Cash App gross profit increased 27%, and Square’s gross payment volume grew 14%.

Those strong results prompted management to raise its 2026 financial guidance. The company now expects full-year gross profit of approximately $12.63 billion, representing 22% growth.

Shares have gained more than 30% in the last year and recently reached a new 52-week high (although they’re almost 68% below the all-time highs set in 2021).

Unity Software (U)

Unity Software (U) has been one of the more dramatic turnaround stories in technology.

The company provides software that developers use to create video games and other interactive experiences. It also operates an advertising platform that helps game publishers attract users and generate revenue.

After several difficult years, Unity is showing signs that its turnaround is gaining traction.

Its third-quarter revenue jumped 32% to $622.1 million. More impressively, the company reported its first quarterly GAAP profit since going public.

A major contributor was Unity Vector, its AI-powered advertising technology, which grew 126% year over year.

Vector uses machine learning to improve advertising performance by helping identify the users most likely to engage with an ad or make a purchase, and it’s the reason for the last bout of outperformance.

The stock has gained 20.6% in the last year and just tagged new 52-week highs (although, like Block, shares are well below all-time highs, down 73.5% in the last five years).

The AI Correction Is Creating New Opportunities

The recent technology selloff is primarily hitting the beneficiaries of the AI data center buildout as fears of more stringent regulation, tighter purse strings and overspending weigh on those names.

Investors are ready to move on to the next stage: companies that are actually deploying AI to improve profitability.

Whether that translates to a durable advantage is yet to be seen (and will probably take at least a few quarters of earnings results to suss out).

And there’s no guarantee that these early winners will prove to be long-term winners.

But outperformance in a correction (relative strength) is a powerful trait, and these five tech stocks are the big winners on that front.

[author_ad]

data.title: Tread Lightly with Broken AI Stocks
data.description:
Note: For a special video version of Mike’s Cabot Wealth Daily article, “Tread Lightly with Broken AI Stocks,” click here.

“Markets are never wrong; opinions are.”

The above quote came from Jesse Livermore, the infamous trader/plunger/speculator of the early 20th century. To this day, many (including myself) consider Reminiscences of a Stock Operator, a slightly fictionalized biography of Livermore under the name Larry Livingston, the best investing book ever written—highly recommended if you haven’t read it yet.

That said, the above quote came from Livermore’s short book How to Trade in Stocks, which is also a great, quick read and reveals a few tidbits about how he operated back in the day. We had this inscription carved into the mantle of the fireplace in our old office so all of us analysts wouldn’t forget it!

Of course, the quote isn’t to be taken literally: There are obviously times when, say, a stock will tank for months only to reverse higher and recapture lost ground. But the main idea was to avoid arguing with the market—whether amateur or professional—that’s how many investors take on heavy losses, including some of the biggest blowups in history.

I was thinking of this quote recently as we’ve seen the sloppy action in most growth areas turn ugly, especially in tech and AI sectors—frankly, a lot of well-known leaders look intermediate- to longer-term toppy, and some are already slicing through long-term support (40-week moving averages, etc.) and are massively off their highs …

… and yet, at the same time, the firms themselves continue to announce amazing results while often sticking with or raising their multi-year forecasts. Wall Street analysts agree, with growth at most top AI firms expected to remain rapid through 2027, if not much longer. And all that means something has to give: For many fundamentally leading AI names, the valuations are getting very, very tame, especially compared to the expected growth rates.

To be clear, I’m not a valuation guy, but the point is that the market (driven by big investors) is clearly forecasting some sort of AI slowdown or even bust phase starting in the next couple of quarters—while company managements and Wall Street analysts see the historic buildout continuing.

[text_ad]

Take Broadcom (AVGO), one of the leaders in the AI chip space and part of the trillion-dollar market cap club. Growth has obviously been hot (sales up 86%, earnings up 96% in the July quarter), but the top brass says it has a “line of sight” for $230 billion of revenues in fiscal 2028, up from an expected $106 billion this year, with earnings exceeding $30 per share, vs. $11.70 or so seen this year! And yet the stock looks awful, below its 40-week line, no higher than it was 14 months ago and trading at just 17x this coming year’s earnings estimates.

Seagate Technology (STX), one of the two leading plays in hard disk drives, is even more dramatic. In the just-reported September quarter (fiscal Q1 for Seagate), sales (up 61%) and earnings (up 194%) growth remained in the stratosphere, and management said it expects this fiscal year (ending next June) to see meaningfully higher growth than last year; analysts see revenues booming 55%. Meanwhile, the top brass said the vast majority of demand is locked in through calendar 2028 (!), with some deals extended to 2030. But, of course, the stock has tanked, breaking down from a multi-month pattern (nearly 50% off its peak) as it trades at just over 9x earnings estimates for the fiscal year ending next June!

Even lesser-known AI winners are seeing the same pattern. Take TTM Technologies (TTMI), a maker of specialized circuit boards; it does good business in aerospace and defense, but data center demand has kicked growth into overdrive during the past year. And after the recent Q3 report, management remained very bullish, thanks in part to booming orders (more than twice output) and backlog (up more than 100%)--analysts see 2027 bringing sales and earnings growth of nearly 50% and 70%, respectively. But, as with the others, TTMI looks like death, sitting more than 60% off its high, below its 40-week line and trading at less than 10x 2027’s earnings estimates.

My main point in bringing up this topic is simply to highlight the dramatically different viewpoints from the two competing sides—it’s obvious big investors are discounting some sort of mini (or larger) AI slowdown, while analysts and most management teams are saying full speed ahead.

I would expect the tension between the stocks and the numbers to be resolved relatively soon—either some of these names will see big rallies, or analysts are going to have to slash outlooks as reality changes. The most important thing is to remain flexible, but for now anyway, you know my take: In the moment, the market is never wrong, so while bounces are possible/likely, it’s best to tread lightly with these damaged stocks.

[author_ad]

data.title: What the Bond Market Is Telling Us About Leading AI Stocks
data.description:
Most stock traders never look at the credit markets. But right now, the credit market is showing some signs of concern, and everyday investors should be listening, especially as AI stocks have been under selling pressure.

So let’s break down what the credit markets are saying for speculative (CRWV), middle-of-the-road (ORCL) and “safe” (META, GOOG) stocks …

What Is a Credit Default Swap?

A credit default swap (CDS) is insurance on a company’s debt. It’s quoted in basis points (1 bp = 0.01%), so a 100-bp spread costs $100,000 a year to insure $10 million of debt. The higher the number, the more worried the market is. And bond investors tend to spot trouble before stock investors do, which makes CDS one of the best early warning systems an everyday investor can watch.

Options traders will appreciate this: A CDS is essentially a put option on a company’s debt.And since bondholders get paid before stockholders, when credit gets nervous, stocks feel it.

[text_ad]

The Speculative Stock: CoreWeave (CRWV)

CoreWeave’s five-year CDS hit a record on October 15 of about $1 million a year to insure $10 million of its debt. S&P Global Market Intelligence estimates that implies roughly a 64% chance of default over five years. That’s a market-implied number, not a forecast, but the bond market is clearly treating CRWV as a speculative credit, with its 2031 bonds yielding 14% to 16% in mid-October.

And not surprisingly, because of these perceived risks, CRWV stock is trading at a multi-year low.

The Middle Ground: Oracle (ORCL)

Think of a credit rating as a report card for borrowers. Oracle still has a passing grade, what Wall Street calls “investment grade,” but just barely. In July, S&P lowered Oracle to BBB-, the last passing grade before “junk.”

The bond market is even more skeptical. Insuring $10 million of Oracle’s debt now costs about $292,000 a year, more than triple what it cost a year ago. That’s the kind of price usually reserved for junk-rated companies.

Why the worry? Oracle has borrowed heavily to build AI data centers and now owes about $125 billion. And on Monday it said it plans to raise another $20 billion by selling new stock and bonds.

Watch Oracle’s CDS like a thermometer. If it keeps rising and Oracle gets downgraded to junk, many bond funds that can only own investment-grade debt would be forced to sell, and that pressure could spill into the stock.

The “Safe” Stocks: Meta (META) and Alphabet (GOOG)

Even the strongest names in tech are seeing record insurance costs. Insuring $10 million of Meta’s debt cost about $119,000 a year at its late-October peak. For Alphabet, Google’s parent company, that cost has nearly tripled in a year to about $92,000.

But those numbers are a fraction of the more than $1 million it costs to insure the same amount of CoreWeave debt, so it’s not as if traders are racing to buy insurance on the slight chance that Meta and Google are going out of business.

Still, Alphabet just had its worst day ever on October 29, falling 12.6% after reporting that it spent more cash than it brought in last quarter, so it’s possible that traders are getting concerned about the company’s spending now and in the future.

Don’t Trade CDS, But Watch Them

The CDS market is often the canary in the coal mine, and right now that market is getting a bit worried about the spending and future of leading AI companies.

Now you don’t need to trade CDS to use them. Instead, check them like a weather report, and when the forecast turns stormy, make sure you have an exit plan for your stock and options positions.

[author_ad]

data.title: Simple vs. Exponential Moving Averages: What’s the Difference?
data.description:
If you’ve given any thought to technical analysis as part of your investing journey, you’ve undoubtedly come across references to moving averages. They’re frequently covered in the mainstream financial press, they’re a default setting on many charting tools, and we regularly use moving averages here at Cabot (both the Cabot Tides and the Cabot Trend Lines in Cabot Growth Investor rely on moving averages).

In fact, you may have read about the importance of the 200-day moving average on the pages of the Cabot Wealth Daily.

In the case of Cabot’s use of moving averages and default chart settings (at least for Yahoo! Finance or stockcharts.com, shown below), what you’re encountering are simple moving averages (SMAs).

What you may be less familiar with are exponential moving averages (EMAs), which use a different calculation than simple moving averages to give more weight to recent price movements. While SMAs are far more common, EMAs are used in a number of valuable studies and are sometimes preferred by high-paced traders. So, let’s break down SMAs vs. EMAs below.

[text_ad]

Simple Moving Averages (SMAs) vs. Exponential Moving Averages (EMAs)

Simple Moving Averages (SMAs)

As you can see in the top left, the moving average line corresponds with “MA(number)”. That means you’re seeing a moving average, with the number (in this case 50 or 200) representing the number of periods used to calculate the average.

MA(200) on a daily chart would be a 200-day moving average. MA(200) on an hourly chart would be a 200-hour moving average.

This is why you’ll get different values if you change time periods on your charts. To see a 200-day moving average on a weekly chart, for instance, you’d use a 40-period (40 weeks x 5 days/week = 200 days) moving average.

The calculation is straightforward. For a 50-day moving average, the closing price for each of the last 50 days is added together and then divided by 50. When you reach a new day (day 51), the earliest value (day 1) drops off and the new day is added, but the denominator remains the same.

That’s why you’ll see an upward-sloping moving average line when a stock price is moving higher, and a downward-sloping line when a stock price is moving lower. But, the simplicity of that calculation also introduces something called “lag,” which is when a moving average is still heading higher while a stock price may have reversed course, or vice versa.

If, for example, the closing price on day 51 is lower than day 50 (stock price headed lower) but still above the closing price of day 1, your moving average will keep heading higher because the day 1 value has been replaced with the higher day 51 value in the calculation.

You can see that in April and October on the chart above when the Dow begins stringing together higher closes but the 50-day SMA keeps trending lower.

This lag isn’t all bad. It can help discount market noise and can keep you from getting knocked out of a promising stock because of short-term volatility, but it’s also why many day traders prefer to use EMAs for entry and exit points.

Exponential Moving Averages (EMAs)

The exponential moving average, on the other hand, uses slightly more complicated calculations to give more weight to recent price movements. This is done through the use of a “smoothing factor” (usually 2) that determines how much extra weight to give to the most recent close.

In a 50-day EMA with a smoothing factor of 2, the most recent close represents 3.9% of the total value of the EMA, and the other 49 days comprise the remaining 96.1%.

We won’t get into the math here, but a smoothing factor of 3 would give the most recent close a 5.9% weight on a 50-day EMA. The higher your smoothing factor, the closer you get to just replicating the price chart.

Because the EMA is calculated by adding the most recent day’s value (prior close x 3.9%) to the previous day’s modified EMA (yesterday’s EMA x 96.1%), that extra weight in the most recent days is “sticky,” for lack of a better term (the day before the prior close is 3.9% of the 96.1% balance, or 3.75% of the total EMA). The end result is that an exponential moving average responds more quickly to price movements, as you can see below.

The EMA on that chart (green line) turns down more sharply in March but then starts trending higher (in April) several weeks before the SMA turns upward (in May), all because it’s valuing the recent uptrend more highly. By that same token, a trader using EMA instead of the SMA would have gotten a “break” above the moving average a day earlier.

But it works the same way in either direction, which makes it more susceptible to false breakouts (or breakdowns).

The tradeoff, as with most indicators, is speed for stability. A faster signal from an EMA is more likely to be wrong than a slower signal from an SMA with the same period. The upside is you’re in and out quicker (more gains, fewer losses) but the downside is more false starts.

The most important takeaway is that the indicator you use should match your trading style and personal preferences. If you’re an intermediate- or long-term investor who wants to be aware of the technical picture (without necessarily trading off it), the SMA is the safer bet (plus, it’s the moving average you’re most likely to encounter in the media, on charts, etc.).

If, on the other hand, you’re a high-frequency trader who’s regularly in and out of positions and looking for an edge to squeeze out a few more percentage points, the EMA may be the way to go.

[author_ad]

*This post has been updated from an original version.

data.title: 3 Best Consumer Staples ETFs to Buy as Inflation Rises
data.description:
I’m not telling you anything new; rising prices are putting a big dent in our pocketbooks.

And with essentials like housing, transportation and food accounting for such a large share of household budgets, even modest price increases can put additional pressure on consumers.

According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), Americans spend their money across the following major categories:

  • Housing: 33.9% of total spending (including rent, utilities and household operations)
  • Transportation: 16.5% (including vehicle purchases, gasoline, public transit and vehicle maintenance)
  • Food: 13.0% (including groceries and dining out)
  • Personal Insurance and Pensions: 12.4%
  • Healthcare: 8.0%
  • Entertainment: 5.0%
  • Apparel and Services: 2.5%

Housing is the single largest household expense, followed by transportation and food. Together, these three categories account for more than 63% of consumer spending. Housing and food alone represent nearly 47%.

That leaves relatively little room in the average household budget to absorb rising prices, particularly when the cost of necessities continues to climb.

Further boosted by September’s 3.7% inflation rate (up from 3.4% in August), total U.S. consumer spending (measured as Personal Consumption Expenditures, or PCE) reached $16.9 trillion in the third quarter of 2026. That’s a sharp rise from full-year 2024 PCE spending of $19.9 trillion.

Although spending on luxury goods and travel is still increasing for the wealthy (who are benefiting from record stock market gains), the rising costs of essentials like gas and food are decreasing the available dollars for regular folks to have fun, led by the escalating price of oil:

  • Gasoline: Jumped 9.1% in September and 34.2% over the last 12 months, accounting for over half of the overall monthly increase in consumer prices.
  • Fuel Oil: Increased significantly by 74.2% year over year.
  • Overall Energy Index: Rose 5.2% in September alone.
  • Shelter / Housing: Rose 0.4% in September and is up 3.2% over the past year.

As a result, consumers are tightening their belts on spending on discretionary retail, expensive hobbies, and travel and are turning toward more frugal fun like staycations and do-it-yourself hobbies.

And a further sad consequence of all of these rising costs is that consumer debt has been mounting, reaching $18.8 trillion in the second quarter, with credit card/bankcard balances representing $1.26 trillion (up $21 billion or +1.7% in Q2, nearing the all-time peak of $1.28 trillion, and up $54 billion from a year earlier).

data.title: Anthropic’s S-1: The Case Studies Tell the Tale
data.description:
On October 26, Anthropic filed its S-1 with the SEC.

At the time, it was investors’ most detailed look at the company’s overall business conditions, financials, risk factors, etc.

It showed a company with rapidly growing revenues, a positive Adjusted Operating Margin, and large net losses due to changes in the fair value of convertible notes (the company’s private valuation has grown as Anthropic’s IPO approaches, which creates a non-cash accounting charge).

In the original S-1, which reflected 2026 figures through only the first two quarters of the year, first-half revenue rose from $1.2 billion to $16.3 billion year over year, Adjusted Operating Margin rose from -159% to 10%, and the accounting-driven net loss rose from $13.0 billion to $80.7 billion.

Absent from the S-1 were the long-term obligations Anthropic has incurred to secure compute resources and infrastructure, which were widely understood to be in the hundreds of billions of dollars.

Then, on November 2, Anthropic filed an amended S-1 with the SEC that cracked the door open a bit further.

The amended filing, which also included Q3 figures, showed total year-to-date revenue of $33.2 billion—with $16.9 billion coming in Q3 alone—a last-nine-month Adjusted Operating Margin of 12%, and a nine-month net loss of $104.0 billion.

More importantly, it also revealed that Anthropic has $895 billion in commitments through 2045, with nearly $450 billion coming due by the end of 2030.

The cost of those commitments may well be enough to keep Anthropic from achieving profitability. As noted in the S-1, Risk Factors, they “have a history of net losses and may not generate sufficient revenue to achieve or sustain profitability in the future.”

[text_ad]

That is, in Anthropic’s defense, a bit of boilerplate for the filing, but they’ve “incurred net losses in each year since [their] founding,” and the scale of their ongoing spending obligations reflects what is increasingly an all-or-nothing bet on artificial intelligence.

The Verge put it best in a November 2 headline: “Anthropic’s business plan: Build God or die trying.”

The expenditures make it abundantly clear that Anthropic is not concerned about short- or intermediate-term fluctuations in profitability; the company is going all-in on building some form of general-purpose AI superintelligence, come what may.

They allude to it in the S-1 filing when highlighting what they see as their “Total Addressable Market” (i.e., where they see an opportunity to generate revenue).

Specifically, Anthropic highlights the opportunity in “knowledge work” (on page 189 of the amended S-1):

“We believe the work that knowledge workers perform represented more than $40 trillion in economic value globally in 2025, and with frontier AI’s potential to make them meaningfully more productive, our near-term opportunity is to expand this value and accelerate economic growth.”

That $40 trillion figure dwarfs the only other economic opportunities Anthropic cites in the S-1: cybersecurity (Grand View Research estimates that the cybersecurity market is $302 billion this year) and life sciences (Anthropic’s S-1 calls out $2 trillion in spending by pharmaceutical companies this year).

If increasing the productivity of knowledge workers (or replacing them) is the profit opportunity—and if it’s the justification for planning nearly half a trillion dollars in spending in the next four years—it stands to reason that we should assess Anthropic’s prospects for success or failure based on progress on that front.

So, how’s that going?

Based on the case studies included in the S-1, not well.

Beginning on page 208 of the original filing (and page 211 of the amended filing), Anthropic outlines the successes that their own clients have had as a result of implementing Anthropic’s AI tools.

While the results from efforts in the software/cybersecurity and life sciences fronts are impressive, results from other segments of the economy are anything but.

To wit, the case study with Bristol-Myers Squibb found that “(t)ime to answer a real-world evidence question” fell from two months to just five minutes, while Salesforce saw its “(e)ffective output per developer year over year” rise by 151% when using Claude Code.

At the same time, PayPal’s “(a)verage time saved per sales employee per week” clocked in at a paltry 45 minutes, while Legora found a time savings of 4.3 “(n)on-billable hours recaptured per lawyer weekly, in an independent study of 31 firms.”

Similarly, the International Rescue Committee, in a 300-user pilot, netted 464 “staff hours returned per week,” or 1.55 hours per user.

And while Anthropic highlighted a case study conducted with Accenture that netted a 7x return on investment (ROI) for “a broadband provider that is a joint Accenture and Anthropic customer” (presumably this case study with Cox Communications), Accenture itself has subsequently capped its own Claude spending at $29 per month per employee. Although it’s worth pointing out that employees can spend more than that limit if they attribute it to a specific internal cost center to justify the use.

In the aggregate, these case studies paint what I consider to be a fairly clear picture of Anthropic’s offerings: Claude and Claude Code are impressive tools for a narrow slice of industry-specific applications while offering little more than limited productivity gains for knowledge workers at large.

Unless and until that changes, and to paraphrase The Verge, it seems that Anthropic is far more likely to “die trying” than they are to “build God,” which leaves the AI bubble on borrowed time.

data.title: How to Evaluate Growth Stocks: 6 Ways to Look Beyond the Hype
data.description:
To evaluate a growth stock, examine five things: sustainable revenue growth, customer demand, improving profitability, a defensible competitive advantage, and evidence that could invalidate your investment thesis. Then assess whether the valuation and stock-price trend support buying. An exciting story alone is not enough.

Growth stocks can certainly be exciting—and that can be a problem.

The best stories usually involve huge markets, innovative products and eye-catching revenue growth. When a stock is moving higher, it’s easy to imagine just how big the company might become.

Investors face a constant stream of optimistic forecasts from experts, influencers, pundits, and promoters competing for attention. We are awash in breathless, overly optimistic forecasts, predictions, and hype from influencers and pundits competing for viewers and readers, as well as marketers trying to sell you something.

But a great story doesn’t necessarily make a great investment. In fact, the most exciting stocks often carry the highest expectations, which means they also have plenty of room to disappoint.

So, before buying a growth stock, you need to look past the headlines and determine whether the underlying business can support the story—and the valuation.

Evaluation QuestionEvidence to ExamineWarning Signs
Is growth sustainable?Revenue trends, organic growth, customer concentrationAcquisition-driven growth masking weak underlying demand
Do customers value the product?Retention, repeat purchases, customer spendingRising churn or discount-dependent sales
Are the economics improving?Margins, cash flow, dilutionPersistent losses without improving economics
Is the advantage defensible?Pricing power, switching costs, market shareCompetitive pressure eroding margins or retention
What would invalidate the thesis?Written expectations and sell criteriaDeteriorating results or a broken price trend

Here are the six questions to ask.

Six Questions to Ask When Evaluating Growth Stocks

Is the Company Producing Real, Sustainable Growth?

Sustainable growth comes from repeatable customer demand and a business that can expand over time. Examine revenue across several quarters, separate organic growth from acquisitions, and compare results with industry trends.

Start with revenue. One strong quarter is encouraging, but it doesn’t tell you much by itself. Ideally, you want to see attractive sales growth over several quarters and, when possible, several years.

Ask:

  • Is revenue growth accelerating, holding steady or slowing?
  • Is growth coming from stronger demand, acquisitions, or price increases?
  • Does the company depend heavily on one product or customer?
  • Is the potential market large enough to support years of expansion?

At Cabot, we use what we call SNaC analysis – Story, Numbers and Chart.

Cabot FrameworkWhat Investors Examine
StoryCustomer need, market opportunity, management, and competitive advantage
NumbersRevenue, margins, cash flow, valuation, and dilution
ChartPrice trends, trading volume, and market response to results

The source of the growth matters. Let’s take two hypothetical companies. A company growing revenue 25% because more customers are buying its core products may have a stronger business than one growing 40% mainly through acquisitions, heavy promotions, or steep discounts.

Industry comparisons help, too. A software company growing 20% in a market expanding 5% is probably gaining share. A company growing at the same rate in a market expanding 30% may actually be losing ground.

Simply put, you want growth that is both strong and repeatable.

Do Customers Really Value the Product?

Every growth story eventually comes back to the customer.

Look for rising customer counts, strong retention, repeat purchases, higher revenue per customer and expanding subscription contracts. These indicators help separate products with lasting value from those benefiting from temporary enthusiasm.

The right metrics will vary by industry. For subscription businesses, annual recurring revenue, churn and net revenue retention can be revealing. For retailers and restaurants, comparable-store sales and store-level economics matter. For consumer platforms, engagement may tell you more than the number of registered accounts.

After all, a company can boast about millions of users, but inactive accounts don’t produce much economic value.

The real question is straightforward: Are customers adopting the product, continuing to use it and spending more over time?

If the answer is yes, the growth story has substance. If not, you may be looking at hype.

Is the Growth Becoming More Profitable?

Many young growth companies willingly sacrifice current earnings to develop products, attract customers and expand into new markets. That’s not automatically a warning sign. Many very successful growth stocks are companies that lost enormous sums of money for many years. But the economics should improve as the business gets bigger.

Watch gross margin, operating margin and free cash flow. If revenue is rising quickly but losses are expanding just as fast, the company may be buying growth rather than building a durable business.

What you want to see is operating leverage—revenue growing faster than expenses, allowing margins to improve over time. The company doesn’t need to be profitable today, but there should be a credible path to profitability.

Also pay attention to stock-based compensation. Companies frequently exclude this expense from “adjusted” earnings, but it is a real cost to shareholders because issuing additional shares dilutes their ownership. Compare adjusted results with generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) earnings and track the share count over time.

Free cash flow offers another useful reality check, but working-capital timing, capital spending, and stock-based compensation can complicate interpretation. Earnings include estimates and accounting judgments. Cash flow provides a clearer indication of whether the business is starting to finance its own operations.

Does the Company Have a Defensible Advantage?

A defensible competitive advantage helps a company retain customers and protect its economics as rivals enter the market. Look for evidence in retention, pricing power, market share, and margins.

Fast growth attracts competition. If a company has found an attractive market, you can assume other businesses will come after it.

The question is what prevents those rivals from copying the product, cutting prices or taking customers.

Potential competitive advantages include the following:

  • Proprietary technology or intellectual property
  • Network effects
  • High switching costs
  • A trusted brand
  • Economies of scale
  • Exclusive data or distribution
  • Regulatory approvals or other barriers to entry

Don’t simply accept management’s claims about its competitive position. Look for proof in customer retention, market-share gains, profit margins, and pricing power.

A genuine advantage should show up in the results.

Management matters as well. Strong executives allocate capital carefully, communicate candidly, and balance long-term ambition with financial discipline. Earnings-call transcripts and shareholder letters can tell you a lot. Pay attention to whether management addresses setbacks directly or repeatedly blames outside conditions.

Insider ownership can help align executives with shareholders. Strong buying by insiders is usually a positive sign. And, while heavy insider selling or repeated share issuance may be the result of many factors, it deserves a closer look.

What Would Prove the Investment Thesis Wrong?

Before buying, write down why you expect the stock to succeed—and what evidence would tell you that you’re wrong.

Warning signs could include slowing customer growth, rising churn, deteriorating margins, growing debt, lost market share, management turnover or a broken price trend.

Defining those risks in advance makes it easier to act rationally when conditions change.

Position sizing is part of that discipline. Even a thoroughly researched growth stock carries uncertainty, so don’t let one exciting story dominate your portfolio. Establish a loss limit or sell discipline before emotions enter the picture. And you may want to build your position over time, particularly if the stock price has been experiencing volatility.

How Do You Know If a Growth Stock Is Too Expensive?

A great company can still be a poor investment if its stock price assumes near-perfect execution. Even if the answers to the previous 5 questions are positive, if the growth in sales or earnings falls short of forecasts, the stock may decline.

Compare the valuation with expected growth, margins, cash generation, competitors, and the company’s own history. What happens if growth slows or profitability takes longer than expected?

Combine Fundamentals with Market Action

Fundamental analysis can help determine what to own. Technical analysis can help determine when to own it.

The strongest growth stocks often show healthy price and trading-volume action as institutional investors build positions. Conversely, a company may report excellent results while its stock repeatedly fails to respond.

That kind of divergence matters. It can mean expectations are already built into the price—or that investors see trouble ahead.

No single metric will identify every future winner. Instead, assemble the evidence: sustainable revenue growth, satisfied customers, improving economics, a defensible advantage, capable management, a supportable valuation and constructive market action.

At Cabot we talk about story, numbers, and chart (SNaC). The story (management, market opportunity, brand positioning, etc.) and the numbers (sales and earnings trends, ratios, etc.) are the elements of fundamental analysis. The chart (technical analysis) tells you how the market is perceiving the stock.

Growth investing will always involve uncertainty. The goal isn’t to avoid exciting companies. It’s to make sure the business behind the excitement is strong enough to justify your investment.

When the story and the evidence agree, you may have found a genuine opportunity. When they don’t, it usually pays to believe the evidence.

If you prefer to have someone else do this research and analysis for you, that’s what our expert team of investment analysts does.

Cabot has a number of growth-oriented advisory services, including Cabot Growth Investor for mid- and large-cap stocks, Cabot Small-Cap Confidential (self-explanatory), and Cabot Explorer for global growth opportunities.

Growth Stock FAQs:

Can a company be a good growth investment before it becomes profitable?

Yes. An unprofitable company can be an attractive growth investment if it has strong customer demand, improving business economics, and enough cash to fund its operations. Investors should look for a credible path to profitability and a valuation that reflects the risks.

Does rapid revenue growth make a stock a good investment?

No. Rapid revenue growth can mask heavy losses, excessive spending, or reliance on acquisitions and discounts. A good investment also requires durable demand, sound finances, and a reasonable valuation. Even an excellent business can deliver disappointing stock returns if investors pay too much.

How do fundamental and technical analysis work together?

Fundamental analysis evaluates a company’s business, financial performance, and valuation to help determine what to own. Technical analysis examines stock-price trends and trading volume to help guide when to buy or sell. Together, they help investors compare the business’s prospects with the market’s response.

data.title: Stanford Endowment Soars with SpaceX (SPCX)
data.description:
The endowment fund of Harvard surged to a record $68 billion as successful bets on equities and venture capital, including SpaceX (SPCX), helped the richest U.S. college handle an unprecedented pressure campaign from Washington, D.C.

Harvard’s endowment fund returned 27% as donations also rose to $1.5 billion, according to a financial report for the fiscal year ending in June.

These strong gains in the stock market and its hedge fund portfolio allowed Harvard to easily beat the 19% median return before fees for large U.S. college endowments and post its best year since 2021.

But wait. Stanford University, with a 32% return, beat Harvard handily, and the University of Pennsylvania basically tied its performance.

Heading one of these endowments is a hot seat. Harvard’s fund chief is N.P. “Narv” Narvekar, who has been in place for a decade, is ending his career on a high note and has apparently faced some criticism for some investments in private equity.

Endowment gains are crucial to universities as they contend with uncertainty around future government research funding. Cutting costs is also part of the deal; Harvard, for one, froze employee pay.

All the above schools had a solid year due to skilled and perhaps lucky asset allocation with the global perspective that these endowments employ.

What can we learn from these endowments about investing?

[text_ad]

While most individual investors focus on short-term stock picks and chase funds with the highest latest returns, endowments put their energies and resources into asset allocation. By this I mean figuring out what percentage of their capital to put in different buckets of assets such as U.S. or international large-cap and small-cap stocks, real estate, timber, precious metals, energy, different countries, venture capital and private equity.

A key difference is the variety of buckets endowments use to diversify, with the goals of lowering risk and volatility and increasing returns.

Endowment investment returns are critical, as Harvard provided more than $775 million in financial aid and spent $969 million on capital expenditures. Roughly 40% of the university’s operating revenue comes from the endowment.

One edge these endowments have over us mortals is a high allocation to private equity, which grew to 46%. Still, the university maintains significant liquid assets and access to credit lines to supercharge financial flexibility.

Another advantage is that endowments get opportunities to invest in private companies way before they go public. Early-stage investors get in on the game at much lower prices, thus boosting returns considerably as the companies go public. After all, it was a no-brainer that SpaceX would go public at some point.

Stanford may have an edge on Harvard due to its proximity to Silicon Valley and its legions of alumni who become tech mavens, executives, and investors.

Finally, while Harvard held $2 billion in SpaceX shares as of June 3, early investments in SpaceX have fueled stellar gains at a handful of other endowments, with the University of North Carolina and Washington University posting returns of more than 35% in the most recent fiscal year. I’m sure there are others that did even better, but perhaps they took on more risk?

Endowment returns, like our own, must be evaluated on returns over time as well as year-to-year volatility. One great year cannot be followed by a loser. Even a ten-year time frame is too short.

I would love to know what asset classes, stocks, and funds these endowments are after next. We can all benefit from having the patience and discipline to follow the endowment model.

[author_ad]
